# The agent prompt

In ask mode the agent is told how to use SkillNib by a short note that `nib init claude --mode ask` writes to `.claude/rules/nib.md`. This is the whole note for the five sample skills (with `nib` installed on your path; otherwise the command is written as `node "<path>/nib.js"`):

```text
<!-- Generated by `nib init claude --mode ask`. Remove with: nib init claude --undo -->
# Skills served by SkillNib

These skills are served by SkillNib and are not loaded by Claude Code on its own. Before a task that one of them may cover, run `nib ask "<what you need to know>"` with the Bash tool and follow the sections it returns. Fetch any listed section with `nib show <ref>`. Do not answer such tasks from memory.

Skills:
- acme-commit-messages: Acme's convention for git commit messages. Use when writing a commit message or squash-merge title.
- acme-error-copy: Acme's guidelines for user-facing error messages. Use when writing, reviewing or translating error text shown in the product.
- acme-incident-report: How Acme documents production incidents after they are resolved. Use when writing an incident report, postmortem or outage summary.
- acme-release-notes: How Acme writes, reviews and publishes release notes for its products. Use when drafting or editing release notes or a changelog entry.
- acme-sql-style: Acme's SQL style guide for analytics queries. Use when writing or reviewing SQL against the Acme warehouse.
```

The note lists your skills by name and description (clipped to 160 characters each, and the whole note to 3,000 characters; extra skills are summarised as "and N more" with the command to list them). It is regenerated when you run `nib init claude` again, so do not edit it by hand.

## Using it with another agent

Any agent that can run shell commands can use SkillNib. Put the paragraph below in its instructions file, replacing the skill list with your own:

```text
These skills are served by SkillNib. Before a task that one of them may cover, run `nib ask "<what you need to know>"` with the Bash tool and follow the sections it returns. Fetch any listed section with `nib show <ref>`. Do not answer such tasks from memory.
```

Keep the instruction to the point: when to ask, what to run, what to do with the answer. SkillNib itself adds no instructions to what it returns; it frames each section with its skill and file name and lists what it left out.

## Asking well

`nib ask` matches words, not meaning. It scores every section against the ask with BM25, a word-frequency formula, using the section title and text, and returns the best sections with a score above zero.

- Use the words the skill uses. "Wording of an error message" finds an error-copy skill; "make users less annoyed" may not.
- Be specific. Name the product, command, field or concept you need. Add the situation: "write a squash-merge title" beats "git".
- One need per ask. Ask twice for two topics instead of one long mixed question.
- If nothing matches, `nib ask` says so and prints the list of skills. Rephrase with a word that appears in the skill, or fetch a section with `nib show <ref>`.
- Fetch what was left out. The outline below the sections lists every undelivered section with its reference.

For the agent this means: ask in the words of the task, not in the words of the problem it is solving, and read the outline before assuming a skill has nothing to say.
